Metadata.Summary: Derm Foundation is a machine learning model that generates embeddings for dermatology images. It helps to efficiently build AI models for dermatology image-related tasks, requiring less data and compute than training a model without the embeddings [SOURCE 1].

UsesAndDirections.IntendedUseAndWorkflow: Derm Foundation can reduce the training data, compute, and technical expertise necessary to develop task-specific models for skin image analysis. It can be used for classifying clinical conditions, scoring severity, identifying the body part the skin is from, and determining image quality [SOURCE 4].

Warnings.ModelLimitations: The quality of Derm Foundation can degrade in extreme conditions, such as photos that are too light or too dark. Also, it was trained on data from a limited set of countries and settings, so it may not generalize well to data from other countries, patient populations, or image types not used in training [SOURCE 4].

TrustIngredients.ModelType: The model is a BiT-101x3 CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) [SOURCE 4].
TrustIngredients.FoundationModelsUsedInApplicationIfAppli: Derm Foundation was trained in two stages. The first pre-training stage used contrastive learning to train on a large number of public image-text pairs from the internet. The image component of this pre-trained model was then fine-tuned for condition classification using clinical datasets.
TrustIngredients.TrainingData: Derm Foundation was trained in two stages: first, using contrastive learning on public image-text pairs, and second, fine-tuned for condition classification using clinical datasets from the United States, Colombia, Australia, and additional public images [SOURCE 4].
TrustIngredients.ValidationTestDataset: Derm Foundation was evaluated for data-efficient accuracy across a range of skin-related classifications tasks. Training a linear classifier on Derm-Foundations embeddings were substantially more performant (10-15% increase in accuracy) than doing the same for a standard BiT-M model across different proportions of training data [SOURCE 4].
